rows.name: fifo-why
rows.question: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.answer:
Index equality occurs both when the queue is empty and when it has completed a full lap of the array.

Initially, the capacity-17 state is `head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, count_ = 0`: empty. After 17 successful pushes with no pops, it is `head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, count_ = 17`: full, because `tail_` has wrapped back to zero.

The actual implementation distinguishes these states using `count_`: `pop` rejects when `count_ == 0`, and `push` rejects when `count_ == capacity`. Its invariant is `0 <= count_ <= 17` and `tail_ == (head_ + count_) % 17`, so equal indices alone cannot tell those two states apart.

review.note: Actualhead0/tail0/count0 versus count17, correct modulo invariant and why an extra slot is unnecessary.
review.usefulPrefix:
Index equality occurs both when the queue is empty and when it has completed a full lap of the array. 
Initially, the capacity-17 state is `head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, count_ = 0`: empty.

rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
With IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, both original expressions give 1. For the changed triple, the left grouping gives 0 and the right grouping gives 1.

Original triple:
• `(16777216 + -16777216) + 1`: the first addition gives exactly 0, then the second gives exactly 1.
• `16777216 + (-16777216 + 1)`: the inner sum is exactly -16777215, which is representable; adding 16777216 then gives exactly 1.

Changed triple:
• `(16777216 + 1) + -16777216`: the exact first sum, 16777217, is not representable. At and above 16777216, binary32 spacing is 2, so it lies halfway between 16777216 and 16777218. Ties-to-even rounds it to 16777216; the final addition therefore gives exactly 0.
• `16777216 + (1 + -16777216)`: the inner sum is exactly -16777215. Below magnitude 16777216, spacing is 1, so that integer is representable; the final addition gives exactly 1.

The crucial distinction is that 16777217 is not representable, but -16777215 is.

review.note: Correct original1/1 and changed0/1 with round-nearest ties-even explicitly assumed, representable negative intermediate and positive midpoint explained.
review.usefulPrefix: With IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, both original expressions give 1. For the changed triple, the left grouping gives 0 and the right grouping gives 1.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without read write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: a completed read can see a new version, followed by a nonoverlapping read that sees the old version.

Let all five replicas initially store version 0. Execute these events in order:
1. A writer invokes a write of version 1. A stores it and acknowledges; messages to B,C,D,E are delayed. The write remains incomplete because it has only one acknowledgement.
2. Reader R1 queries A,B,C. Their replies are 1,0,0, so R1 returns 1.
3. After R1 returns, reader R2 starts and queries C,D,E. All reply 0, so R2 returns 0.

To explain R1’s result, any attempted linearization must include the pending write and place it before R1. Real-time order requires R1 before R2, giving write(1) → R1 → R2. With no intervening write, R2 must then return 1, contradicting its actual return of 0. Omitting the pending write cannot explain R1 either.

Read write-back fixes this counterexample, provided the reader waits for acknowledgements from three replicas before returning. If R1 selects version 1 and writes it back to A,B,C, all three hold version 1 or higher when R1 finishes. R2’s query quorum C,D,E intersects that write-back quorum at C, so R2 cannot return version 0. More generally, any two sets of three among five intersect, and replicas never decrease their versions; therefore a completed read establishes a quorum that prevents later reads from going backward, even when the original write is incomplete.

With a single writer assigning increasing versions, this is the standard quorum write-back approach to a linearizable register. If multiple writers are allowed, their version-assignment protocol must also be specified and correct; read write-back alone does not establish that.

review.note: Pending writer stores1 onlyA; R1ABC observes1 then nonoverlapping R2CDE observes0. W<R1<R2 contradicts register semantics; quorum write-back prevents rollback, qualified unique ordered versions/single writer.
review.usefulPrefix:
Without read write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: a completed read can see a new version, followed by a nonoverlapping read that sees the old version. 
Let all five replicas initially store version 0.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because the two reads completed in real-time order: the first read’s response occurs before the second read’s invocation, so any linearization must place R1 before R2.

If R1 returns version 1, the pending write of version 1 must be included and placed before R1 to explain that result. With no intervening write, R2 cannot then return version 0: the required order is W1 < R1 < R2, which makes version 1 the current value at R2.

This does not require every unfinished operation to complete. Linearizability permits pending operations to be omitted or completed in an extension of the history, but this particular write cannot be omitted because a completed read already observed its value.

rows.name: backend-reconnection
rows.question: Why must desired be recomputed after that failure? Refer to the concrete values in the preceding explanation, and state what is retained across a reconnection.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why must desired be recomputed after that failure? Refer to the concrete values in the preceding explanation, and state what is retained across a reconnection.
rows.answer:
After A’s failed CAS, `expected` changes from 0 to 1, so `desired` must be recomputed as 2. Keeping `desired = 1` lets the retry successfully replace 1 with 1, losing A’s increment.

Interpreting “reconnection” as the next retry: the updated `expected = 1` is retained across iterations; the corrected loop computes a fresh `desired = expected + 1`. A spurious failure also retries with the observed `expected`, recomputing `desired` even if `expected` hasn’t changed.

review.note: Recalls actual CAS example after forced backend closure but reinterprets reconnection as retry. Does not answer what conversation state survives transport reconnection; not evidence of RAM loss.
